o: Lord God, Creator of heaven and earth, I thank You for this morning. When I look at the sky, the light of the sun, the clouds and the birds, Your wisdom amazes me. Everything You have made speaks of You, and today I want to listen with an attentive heart. Thank You, because the same God who holds up the stars also cares for me.

Father, sometimes my life fills with noise, tasks and screens, and I forget to look up. Forgive me for thinking that everything depends on me. Teach me to admire Your work, to learn from it and to give You the glory. Give me a curious mind, a humble heart and the patience to seek the truth, knowing that You are the source of all wisdom.

Bless my work and my studies today. May what I do with my hands and my mind honor You and serve others. Take care of my family, and give me eyes to see Your goodness in small things. At the end of the day, may I be able to say, like the psalmist, that Your power is great and Your understanding is beyond measure. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 15, 1630, the astronomer Johannes Kepler died in the city of Regensburg, in the Holy Roman Empire, at the age of 58. He had traveled there to claim a sum of money owed to him, fell ill a few days after his arrival and was buried in the Protestant cemetery of St. Peter, outside the city walls.

Kepler was born on December 27, 1571, and was a man of Lutheran faith. As a young man, he studied at Tübingen with the desire to become a pastor, but his life led him toward the stars. From Tycho Brahe's careful observations of the planet Mars, he discovered that the planets move in ellipses around the Sun, and published these discoveries in his work Astronomia Nova in 1609. In 1619, in his book Harmonices Mundi, he set out his third law of planetary motion.

For Kepler, studying the heavens was not an activity separate from his faith. He believed that God had created the universe with order and that the human mind, made in the image of God, could understand something of that order. That is why he saw science as a way of admiring the Creator.

Kepler also had difficult moments with his Church. For not having fully accepted a doctrine about the Lord's Supper, he was denied communion in Linz and was excluded in 1619. Despite this, he wrote in favor of tolerance among Christians, saying that Christ the Lord was not, and is not, Lutheran, Calvinist or papist.
His life shows that faith and curiosity can walk hand in hand, and that the starry sky can lead us to worship the one who made it.
m.c: Go out today with your gaze lifted and a trusting heart, for the God who orders the stars also orders your steps. May his peace guard your mind and his joy be your strength. Walk without fear: he goes before you.
m: Psalm 147 says something astonishing: God counts the number of the stars and gives all of them names. And right away it adds that his understanding is beyond measure. If the Lord knows and sustains every star, how could he not know your name, your worries today and your needs? Kepler devoted his life to studying the order of the heavens and discovered that this order spoke of the wisdom of its Creator.

Psalm 148 invites the sun, the moon and the stars to praise the Lord, “for he commanded and they were created.” Creation is a silent hymn. We do not need to be scientists to listen to it: it is enough to stop and look. The problem is that we live with our heads down, caught in the trap of the urgent. God left us the sky, the light and the night as daily reminders that he controls everything and that we are worth much more than we think.

There is also a lesson in humility in Kepler's story. He spent years being wrong, redoing calculations and correcting ideas, until he found the real shape of the orbits. Learning takes time and patience. So too our faith grows: with doubts, corrections and questions, but with a sincere desire to know God as he is.

For today, give yourself five minutes to look at the sky, even if only through a window. Give thanks for three things you have seen in creation. If you have tasks that require mental effort, begin them with a brief prayer asking for wisdom. And when you feel small, remember that the Lord who calls the stars by name knows you too.

o: Lord Jesus, I end this day by giving You thanks. Thank You, because You have passed by my side more often than I realized. Thank You for the morning light, for the work of my hands, for the conversations and for every moment You sustained me without my asking.

There are things, Lord, that I do not yet see clearly. There are paths I do not understand and needs I kept silent out of shame. Like Bartimaeus, I want to cry out to You without fear of what others will say: have mercy on me. You know what I need better than I do. Open the eyes of my heart so that I may see Your love and Your answers, and give me the courage to follow You when You call me.

I commend to You tonight those who suffer, those who have no one to listen to them and those who have lost hope. May they feel that You stop for them. Forgive me for the times I stayed silent when I should have prayed. Let me rest without anxiety, and may I rise tomorrow with gratitude and my eyes fixed on You. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: Jesus was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, on his way to Jerusalem. By the roadside sat a blind man named Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, who was begging. Every day was the same for him: darkness, waiting and dependence on others.

When he heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by, he began to cry out: “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” Many rebuked him to silence him, but he cried out all the more: “Son of David, have mercy on me!” Bartimaeus did not let the crowd's rebuke extinguish his faith.

Then Jesus stopped and said to call him. They said to the blind man: “Take heart; get up, he is calling you.” Throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus. That cloak was surely the little he owned, and he left it without hesitation. Jesus asked him: “What do you want me to do for you?” And the blind man answered: “Rabbi, let me recover my sight.”
Jesus said to him: “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” And immediately he recovered his sight and followed Jesus on the way. He went from the roadside to walking with the Master.
The story of Bartimaeus reminds us that Jesus stops for a sincere cry. No matter how many voices order us to be quiet, or how dark the place where we are sitting, the Lord listens and calls.
t.c: Take with you into your rest the certainty that the Lord has listened to you today and will listen to you tomorrow. Let go of your burdens as one leaves an old cloak by the roadside. May his peace cover you and may you wake with new eyes.
m: Bartimaeus had nothing to offer: no money, no influence, no sight. He had only an honest prayer and the decision not to be silent. Sometimes we believe that God listens only to people who are already well put together, but this story says the opposite. Jesus stops precisely for the one who cries out from his need. Beautiful words are not necessary; sincerity is.

Look at how the crowd reacted: he was told to be quiet. Often the voices that discourage us come from outside, but also from within: “It's not worth it,” “God has more important things.” Bartimaeus cried out louder. Persevering faith is not stubbornness; it is the confidence that the Lord listens. If there is something you have stopped asking God for out of weariness, tonight is a good time to ask for it again.

Moreover, when Jesus called him, Bartimaeus left his cloak. To reach Jesus, one must let go of something: an excuse, a grudge, a comfort, an old way of seeing things. And notice Jesus' question: “What do you want me to do for you?” He wants us to name our need. You can answer him clearly and without detours, for what matters to you matters to him.

To close this day, write or say aloud the answer to that question: “Lord, I want you to do for me...” Then ask yourself what cloak you need to leave behind to draw closer to Jesus. End by giving thanks for what you have already seen of his hand today. Bartimaeus, once healed, followed Jesus; may your gratitude lead you to follow him as well.
